stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of chronic alcoholism has not eaten for 10 days. After starting nutritional support, he develops weakness, confusion, and hypophosphatemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Feeding a starved (alcoholic) patient → insulin surge drives phosphate, K⁺ and Mg²⁺ into cells → refeeding syndrome (hypophosphatemia, weakness, confusion).

why.A: May coexist, but the syndrome is refeeding.
why.C: Doesn't explain low phosphate after feeding.

stem: A 58-year-old man develops an enterocutaneous fistula 2 days after surgery for bowel obstruction. The fistula output is <100 mL/day, and the remaining bowel appears normal. He has no fever. What is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: Continue enteral feeding and provide wound care

expl: A low-output (<200 mL/day, here <100) fistula with normal distal bowel, no sepsis or obstruction usually closes spontaneously → continue enteral nutrition, protect the skin, monitor fluids.

why.B: TPN is for high-output fistulas or when enteral feeding fails.
why.C: Surgery is for fistulas that fail to close (usually after 6–12 weeks).

stem: A 40-year-old man with Crohn’s disease underwent a 40 cm small bowel resection 2 years ago. He now presents with chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and signs of malnutrition. What is the most likely cause?
expl: Keyed short bowel syndrome — diarrhoea, weight loss and malnutrition after small-bowel resection. (Strictly, 40 cm is a modest resection — SBS usually needs < 200 cm remaining; terminal ileal loss can also cause bile-acid diarrhoea and B12 deficiency.)

why.C: Adhesive obstruction causes colic and vomiting.
why.D: Bacterial overgrowth is possible (strictures), but the key is SBS.

stem: A patient is diagnosed with mild acute pancreatitis. What is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: TPN, IV fluids, pain control, antibiotics
Enteral feeding, IV fluids, pain control

srcNote: Incomplete recall: the source supplies only options A and B.
expl: Mild AP → IV fluids (LR), analgesia and early enteral (oral) feeding. TPN and prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated.

why.A: TPN and antibiotics are not indicated.

stem: A 55 y/o man who is receiving total parenteral nutrition through the right subclavian PICC for short bowel syndrome developed high temperature (39C). Two blood cultures were positive for staphylococcus aureus. Which of the following is the most appropriate step in management?

opts.t: Remove the PICC, send tip for culture and administer antibiotics
Change the PICC over the wire

expl: S. aureus bacteremia from a central line (PICC) → remove the line (send the tip for culture) and give a long antibiotic course. S. aureus is never a contaminant.

why.B: Exchanging over a wire keeps an infected tract.
why.C: Lock therapy isn't enough for S. aureus.

stem: Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) is associated with which one of these complications?
srcNote: (Nutrition in surgical patients) Source note (Midterm 429 F Q14): other complications: dehydration and electrolyte Imbalances, thrombosis.
expl: TPN's concentrated dextrose commonly causes hyperglycemia (also line sepsis, thrombosis, electrolyte and liver problems).

stem: A 33 y\o man. RTA-victim with isolated head injury remains in coma 5 days after the accident. Which of the following is the most appropriate feeding method in the early stay of management?
srcNote: (Nutrition in surgical patients) Source note (Midterm 429 F Q12): After 5-7 days we think to give nutrition so in these 5 days pt was on IVF, isolated head trauma= doesn’t mean base of the skull fracture so NGT is NOT contraindicated.
expl: A comatose head-injury patient has a working gut but can't swallow → early enteral feeding by nasogastric tube; a gastrostomy is for long-term feeding (weeks), and parenteral nutrition is only when the gut can't be used.

why.A: Peripheral PN is weak and unnecessary with a working gut.
why.B: Gastrostomy is for long-term feeding, not the early phase.
why.C: Central PN carries line and metabolic risks and isn't needed.

stem: A 65 y/o man who is receiving total parenteral nutrition for high output small bowel fistula with persistent hyperglycemia inspite of insulin infusion. Which of the following is the appropriate step in management?
expl: New, persistent hyperglycemia on TPN despite insulin often signals hidden sepsis — look for the source.

why.A: Oral agents are irrelevant on TPN.

stem: A 45-year-old women on TPN for high output small bowel fistula. The TPN has been abruptly stopped, and the patient transferred for abdominal ultrasound. When the patient arrived to the radiology department, she was anxious, irritable, confused and she developed seizure and loss of consciousness. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
srcNote: (Principles of fluids and electrolytes balance in surgical patient)
expl: TPN contains concentrated glucose with high endogenous insulin; abrupt stop → rebound hypoglycemia (anxiety, confusion, seizures, coma).

stem: Caloric intake requirement in burn patients:
srcNote: , calculate it as per curreri formula 25kcal/kg + 40kcal/TBSA% (if pediatric 60kcal/kg) (Burns) Source inconsistency: the marked option does not match the formula quoted in the source explanation. Both are reproduced as written.
expl: Keyed 70 (odd recall). The Curreri formula is 25 kcal/kg + 40 kcal per %TBSA (the doctor corrected it to 20 kcal/kg); children 60 kcal/kg. None of the options matches exactly — the source key is A.

why.B: 40 kcal is the per-%TBSA part of Curreri.

stem: The basal metabolic rate of an obese person in comparison to a normal weight person (same age and gender)?
expl: The absolute basal metabolic rate rises with body size — an obese person has more lean mass (and fat) to maintain, so their BMR is higher than a normal-weight person of the same age and sex. Obesity comes from intake exceeding expenditure, not a low BMR.

why.B: A common myth — absolute BMR is higher.
why.D: Genetics affects weight but isn't an answer to the comparison.

stem: which of the following is the correct way to measure BMI?
expl: BMI = weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared (kg/m²).

stem: An otherwise healthy patient with good nutritional status underwent gynecomastia excision Which of the following wound healing effects would be seen after prescribing multivitamins to the patient?
expl: Vitamin supplements improve healing only if the patient is deficient. In a well-nourished patient they have no effect.

stem: What is the Neuroendocrine response to surgery?
expl: The surgical stress response (cortisol, catecholamines, glucagon, cytokines) causes peripheral insulin resistance, increased gluconeogenesis and hyperglycaemia.

why.A: The response causes hyperglycaemia, not hypoglycaemia.
why.C: Insulin secretion is relatively suppressed early, with resistance at the tissues.

stem: A patient underwent a gastric sleeve surgery 2 years prior and presents today with symptoms of hyperparathyroidism. What is the likely cause?
expl: Sleeve gastrectomy/bariatric surgery reduces calcium and vitamin D absorption → vitamin D deficiency → secondary hyperparathyroidism.

why.C: A consequence of PTH, not a cause.

stem: A mother with a baby with cleft palate presented to you complaining of a problem with feeding for the last 2 - 3 months and failure of gaining weight. Currently, his weight is 5Kg, what is the best choice for this concern to prepare the patient for surgery?
srcNote: (not sure) (Cleft lip) The source explicitly labels its answer as uncertain.
expl: A cleft baby failing to gain weight despite feeding problems needs his nutrition secured before surgery — feeding via a nasogastric tube while feeding technique is optimized. Weight and Hb (Rule of 10s) show readiness for surgery.

why.B: The problem is mechanical feeding, not a primary medical illness.
why.D: Changing formula doesn't fix the poor seal.

stem: Which of the following formulas is used to calculate a person's BMI?
expl: BMI = weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in metres (kg/m²).

stem: Patient with necrotizing pancreatitis. What is the physiological abnormalities?
expl: Severe systemic inflammation → catabolism: increased lipolysis, increased gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance → hyperglycaemia.

stem: A 60 y/o man was admitted with marked weight loss due to carcinoma of the lower esophagus. Which of the following is the appropriate method to improve his nutritional status before surgery?
srcNote: ( Miscellaneous ) Conflicting source keys: the retained preoperative version gives central parenteral nutrition; other recalls give gastrostomy feeding. The original differences are preserved. Other source key (Midterm 429 F Q30): Answer: C (Nutrition in surgical patients) Patient can use his GI system, but it was answered as TPN. In that version: C. Gastrostomy feeding (this is for long TERM). Other source key (Midterm 428 Q6): Answer: C, Patient still can use his GI. In that version: C. Gastrostomy feeding.
expl: Source key: central parenteral nutrition. Reasoning used by the key: an obstructing lower esophageal cancer limits enteral access, and a gastrostomy would damage the stomach needed as the esophageal conduit. (Another version of this question keyed gastrostomy because the gut is usable.)

why.A: Peripheral PN cannot deliver enough calories for marked weight loss.
why.C: Keyed in the 429 version; the stomach is usually preserved for reconstruction.
why.D: A tube may not pass an obstructing tumor.

stem: Which of the following patient will most likely need parenteral nutritional support after surgery?

opts.t: Massive small bowel resection for mesenteric ischemia
Omental patch closure of perforated duodenal ulcer
Right hemicolectomy of carcinoma of the caecum

srcNote: ( Miscellaneous ) Source note (Midterm 429 F Q13): Intravenous feeding is indicated when patients have intestinal failure. Chronic intestinal failure may result from short bowel syndrome, following extensive small bowel resection, extensive small bowel disease, such as Crohn's disease, and motility disorders, such as chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction
expl: Massive small bowel resection leaves too little absorptive surface (short bowel syndrome) → parenteral nutrition is needed; the other operations leave a functioning gut that recovers within days.

stem: Which of the following represents the physiological action of ghrelin?
expl: Ghrelin, secreted mainly by the gastric fundus, stimulates appetite — the "hunger hormone"; levels rise before meals.

why.A: Satiety is signalled by leptin, PYY and GLP-1.

stem: A 65 y\o man, presented to outpatient clinic complaining of epigastric pain and early satiety for 3 months. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed antral gastric mass. Confirmed by biopsy and histopathology to be adenocarcinoma. Patient was consented for surgery.Which of the following low blood level is suggestive of nutritional deficiency?
expl: Serum albumin is the standard laboratory marker of nutritional status before surgery — a low level (< 3.5 g/dL, or < 3.0 g/dL as severe) predicts more complications and poor healing.

why.B: Magnesium is an electrolyte, not a nutritional marker.
why.C: Transferrin (and prealbumin) also reflect nutrition, but albumin is the classic answer; transferrin also rises with iron deficiency, so it isn't reliable here.
why.D: Low iron in gastric cancer mostly reflects chronic blood loss, not general nutrition.

stem: Body's metabolic response to starvation results in which of the following?

opts.t: Glucagon secretion increases to maintain blood glucose level.
The brain shifts to ketones as primary source of energy during the early response to starvation.
Muscle breakdown is accelerated to provide substrate for gluconeogenesis.
Nitrogen loss in urine is significantly increased.

expl: In starvation, falling glucose raises glucagon (and lowers insulin) to maintain blood glucose through glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. The ketone shift happens late (adaptation), not early, and protein breakdown and nitrogen loss fall as the body adapts.

why.B: Ketones become the brain's main fuel only after days to weeks.
why.C: Protein breakdown is early; with adaptation it is reduced to conserve muscle.
why.D: Nitrogen loss falls in prolonged starvation (unlike injury).

stem: A 29 y/o male sustained massive injury following a motor vehicle collision. When describing his body's response to injury V.S starvation, the body's response to injury is characterized by:

opts.t: A decrease in resting metabolic rate.

expl: Injury causes hypermetabolism and catabolism — increased protein breakdown with high urinary nitrogen loss — whereas starvation adapts by conserving protein and lowering metabolic rate.
